study.title: Psalm 84 - The desire for the presence of God
study.overview: This psalm expresses an intense longing for God's presence in his sanctuary and shows that true bliss is not only about being near the temple, but in trusting the Lord who inhabits and sustains his people. The psalmist values the courtyards of the Lord, wishes to participate in the worship, observes the happiness of those who serve there continuously and ends by affirming that the man who trusts in God is truly happy. The whole of the Psalm unites yearning, prayer, pilgrimage and trust.

outline.title: Burning Desire for the House of God
outline.explanation: The psalmist describes the beauty of the Lord's dwellings and the hunger of his soul for the divine presence. He compares the happiness of those who inhabit God's house with that of birds who find a safe place to live near the altars.

outline.title: The Happiness of those Walking with God
outline.explanation: Here appear those who find strength in the Lord and keep in their hearts the right way. Even going through the arid valley, they turn it into a source, following from force to strength until they appear before God in Zion.

outline.title: Prayer, trust and true bliss
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks God to hear his prayer and see his anointed. He then states that one day in the courtyards of the Lord is worth more than a thousand outside them, because the Lord is sun, shield, grace, honor, and good for those who walk in integrity.

study.context: The title associates the psalm with the children of Coré and the regent, indicating liturgical use. The notes provided highlight that the psalmist is far from the temple and speaks from this absence, as someone who longs to return to public worship. Matthew Henry suggests that psalm may have been written in a time of forced removal from the holy city, but this remains an interpretive reading, not a sure data of the text. Notes also note that references to the temple cover the places of worship and not just a unique space.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that the presence of God is the supreme good of his people. The temple, with its courtyards and altars, points to God himself, and not just for a sacred construction. Biblical happiness is defined as closeness to the Lord, continual praise, strength received from him and trust in him. The text also shows that the pilgrimage of faith includes suffering, but this path can become a source when God grants grace. The image of God as sun and shield brings together provision, protection, life and defense; it is sufficient for all that the faithful need. The conclusion reinforces that trust in God is the centre of true bliss.

scholarViews.insight: The psalmist feels deep longing for God's presence; the temple represents God himself, and the final longing is for him, not just by the building.
The psalmist is deprived of public worship and, therefore, begins to perceive with even more intensity the value of the ordinances of God and of communion with him.
The Lord's Valentines encompass the various places of worship in the temple; the image communicates that the whole sacred area is precious because in it God is worshipped.

questions: What does the fact that I consider the presence of God more valuable than any other place or conquest?
Have I seen the difficulties of the way as a reason for removal or as an opportunity for God to turn the valley into a source?
Is my practical trust in the Lord as a sun, shield, grace and honor, or in other security?
study.practice: Sept time to desire God's presence with honest words, as the psalmist does. Reassess your priorities of worship, prayer and fellowship: ask yourself whether you treat the presence of the Lord as something central or accessory. In the midst of an arid phase, pray asking God to turn his valley into a source and give strength to continue walking with integrity. Practice concrete trust: give the Lord a specific concern and remember again that bliss does not depend on perfect circumstances, but on trusting in him.
study.uncertainty: It is not possible to affirm with historical certainty, only based on the notes provided, who composed the psalm or in which specific episode it was written. Matthew Henry's note about David and the possible escape from Absalom is an interpretative hypothesis. There is also some uncertainty in the observations about verse 11, because Adam Clarke's note mentions that old versions understand the word differently from "sol," so the image should be read with caution, even if the biblical text presented uses this translation.
